thread: Is it a mercy to wake someone to the truth?
summary: Each piece asks whether telling people what they cannot bear to know is a kindness or a cruelty. Lu Xun puts it as an iron house full of sleepers who will suffocate, and asks whether shouting to wake a few only gives them the pain of knowing, then is talked out of his own doubt by hope. Gray watches boys at play, lists every sorrow coming for them, and ends by wondering why they should be told, which is also what the poem has just done. Hawthorne dramatises a man who sees the hidden evil of everyone he loves in one night in the forest, and who can never unsee it, whether or not it was a dream. Simon and Garfunkel sing around it: a speaker with a warning in a crowd that will not listen, and a message left where nobody reads it.

pieces.essay: Lu Xun argues it: the sleeper who is woken only learns he is dying, and the writer who wakes him has to decide whether hope is reason enough.
pieces.poem: Gray images it: children at play in front of all the griefs lined up for them, and a speaker who tells us and then wishes he hadn't.
pieces.story: Hawthorne dramatises it: Brown learns what his town is really like and the knowledge poisons the rest of his life, even though he can't prove it was real.
pieces.song: Simon and Garfunkel sing around it: the warning is given, and the song is about the people who hear it and do nothing.

forYou: In When Jasmine Blooms, the buried history of 1950s Malaya is what the present-day characters have to be woken to, so the question of what that knowledge costs them, and whether the telling is kind, is one the show can ask openly.
